context.transcript:
You will hear eight short recordings. For each question, choose the correct answer.

One. You hear a conversation at a railway station.
W: Excuse me, when is the next train to Samarkand?
M: Let me check. I'm afraid the 2.15 has just left. The next one departs at 2.30 from platform four.
W: That's fine. How long does the journey take?
M: Just over two hours, so you'll arrive at about 4.40.

Two. You hear a telephone message.
M: Good morning, this is a message for Ms Karimova from Dr Aliyev's dental clinic. Unfortunately the doctor will be away on Tuesday, so we have had to change your appointment. Could you come on Thursday instead, at the same time, ten o'clock? Please call us back to confirm. Thank you.

Three. You hear two friends deciding where to eat.
M: I'm starving. Shall we get a pizza at Roma's?
W: Roma's is closed on Mondays, remember? What about that new sushi bar next to the cinema?
M: Sushi is a bit expensive... but all right, let's try it. Pizza can wait until the weekend.

Four. You hear a weather forecast on the radio.
W: Good morning, here is today's weather. It will be wet and windy across the region until midday, so don't leave home without an umbrella. During the afternoon, however, the clouds will clear, and we can expect warm sunshine with temperatures of about twenty-five degrees.

Five. You hear a man shopping for clothes.
M: I like this shirt, but the medium feels a bit tight. Do you have it in large?
W: In large we only have blue and white left — the green is completely sold out.
M: That's a pity, green was my first choice. Hmm, white gets dirty so quickly... I'll take the blue one, then.

Six. You hear an announcement at an airport.
W: Attention please. Flight HY six-oh-two to Istanbul has been delayed by forty minutes because of fog. The flight will now board at six fifty from gate twelve — not gate nine as shown on your boarding passes. We apologise for the inconvenience.

Seven. You hear two colleagues talking on Monday morning.
W: How was your weekend? Did you drive to Chirchiq to visit your grandmother in the end?
M: That was the plan, but my car refused to start on Saturday morning. So I stayed at home and finally painted the kitchen instead. Honestly, it looks fantastic now.

Eight. You hear a student talking to a librarian.
M: Excuse me, what time does the library close today?
W: On weekdays we are open until eight, but today is Saturday, so we close at six. And don't forget we are closed all day on Sundays.
M: Six o'clock — right, I'd better hurry then.

context.transcript:
Hello everyone, and thank you for coming to this short information session about Green Valley Summer Camp. Let me give you the key facts.

The camp is set in beautiful countryside in the Chimgan mountains, right next to a large lake, where campers go swimming and kayaking every morning.

We run three sessions each summer. The first begins on the fifteenth of June, the second on the first of July, and the last one on the twentieth of July. Each session lasts twelve days.

The price is two hundred and forty dollars. That might sound like a lot, but it covers accommodation in comfortable wooden cabins, all meals, and transport — a coach picks campers up from the city centre and brings them back at the end of the session.

Now, what should you pack? Summers are hot, so a hat and sun cream are essential. Trainers are fine for most activities, but for the mountain hikes you will definitely need walking boots — ordinary shoes are simply not safe on rocky paths.

Evenings are always fun. From Monday to Thursday we organise games and quizzes in the main hall, and every Friday evening there is a barbecue down by the river, which campers say is the best part of the whole week.

Finally, how to book. Please note that you can no longer book by phone — places must be reserved through the camp's website, where you will also find photos and answers to common questions. Book early: last year every place was gone by the end of April.

context.transcript:
M: Today my guest is wildlife photographer Nilufar Rashidova, whose pictures of snow leopards have appeared in magazines around the world. Nilufar, welcome to the programme.
W: Thank you for inviting me.
M: How did it all begin for you?
W: People assume I studied photography, but actually my degree is in biology. I only picked up a camera seriously when I was working as a ranger in the Ugam-Chatkal national park and realised that nobody was recording the animals we saw there.
M: Snow leopards are famously difficult to photograph. What's the secret?
W: Patience, much more than equipment. My first good leopard picture took me three winters. I use camera traps — small automatic cameras fixed to rocks — because a human sitting in the snow will simply never get close enough.
M: I imagine the hardest part is the cold?
W: Everyone thinks so, but you can dress for cold. The real difficulty is carrying enough batteries. There is no electricity in the mountains, and in low temperatures batteries die twice as fast, so half of my rucksack is always power banks.
M: What do you hope your photographs achieve?
W: I'm not interested in winning prizes. If a farmer sees my photos and decides that a living leopard is worth more to his village than a dead one — through tourism — that is success for me. That's why I give my pictures free of charge to local schools and conservation groups.
M: And what would you say to young photographers who are just starting?
W: Don't buy expensive equipment at the beginning. Learn to sit still and watch. The best camera in the world is useless if you don't understand the animal in front of it.

parts.instructionsEn: You will hear a short talk about the history of paper. Complete the sentences. Write ONE or TWO words for each gap.

context.transcript:
Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about something we all use every day without thinking: paper — and, in particular, the special role our region played in its history.

Paper was invented in China around two thousand years ago. For centuries the Chinese kept the production method a complete secret, and people in other countries had to write on expensive materials such as silk, or on specially prepared animal skin known as parchment.

Everything changed in the eighth century. After a famous battle near the Talas river, craftsmen who knew the secret of paper-making were brought to Samarkand, and the city soon became the paper capital of the Islamic world. Samarkand paper was celebrated for two qualities: it was remarkably smooth, and it was strong — strong enough, in fact, that some documents written on it can still be read today, centuries later.

So what made it so good? The most important ingredient was the bark of the mulberry tree — the same tree whose leaves feed silkworms. The bark was soaked in water, beaten into a soft paste, pressed into thin sheets, and finally each sheet was polished with a smooth stone or a piece of glass until the surface shone.

From Samarkand the technology travelled slowly westwards — first to Baghdad, then to Egypt — and it arrived in Europe only in the twelfth century, roughly four hundred years after it reached our region.

Today you can still watch paper being made in the traditional way. A small workshop near Samarkand, run by a family of craftsmen, produces mulberry paper by hand using water power, and it has become a popular stop for tourists. Artists particularly value this paper because it does not change colour, even after many years.

parts.instructionsEn: You will hear part of a university lecture about sleep. For each question, choose the correct answer.
parts.instructionsUz: Uyqu haqidagi universitet ma'ruzasidan parchani tinglang. Har bir savol uchun to'g'ri javobni tanlang.

context.transcript:
Good morning, everyone. In today's lecture I want to challenge a popular idea: the belief that sleep is simply a period when the brain switches off. Nothing could be further from the truth. In many ways your brain is busier at three in the morning than at three in the afternoon.

Let's start with memory. During the day, new information is stored temporarily in a region called the hippocampus — think of it as a notebook for quick notes. But the notebook is small, and it fills up fast. While you sleep, the brain copies important information from this temporary store into long-term storage in the cortex, and — just as importantly — it deletes what it does not need. This is why students who sleep after studying consistently outperform those who stay up all night revising. In one well-known experiment, participants who slept after learning a list of words remembered about forty per cent more than those who stayed awake.

The second function is physical, and it was only discovered quite recently, in 2013. During deep sleep, the channels between brain cells widen, allowing fluid to wash through the brain and carry away waste chemicals produced during the day. One of these chemicals is linked to Alzheimer's disease, which may explain the connection researchers keep finding between years of poor sleep in middle age and memory problems decades later.

So how much sleep do we actually need? For adults, the evidence points clearly to between seven and nine hours. Some people insist they function perfectly on five. Laboratory testing shows that almost all of them are wrong: their reaction times and judgement decline sharply, but their opinion of their own performance stays high. In other words, sleep-deprived people are usually the last to notice their own mistakes — which is precisely what makes driving while tired so dangerous.

Finally, a word about naps, because they are often dismissed as laziness. A short nap of around twenty minutes measurably improves alertness and mood. The key word is short. Sleep longer than about half an hour in the daytime and you enter deep sleep, and waking from deep sleep leaves you feeling worse than before — slow and confused, a state scientists call sleep inertia. Next week we will look at what happens when we dream.

parts.passageText:
The Silk Road: Past and Present

A. Despite its famous name, the Silk Road was never a single road. It was a huge network of caravan tracks that connected China with the Mediterranean, crossing deserts and mountain passes along the way. Few merchants ever travelled the whole distance of nearly seven thousand kilometres; instead, goods changed hands many times, rising in price at every stop.

B. Silk, of course, moved along these routes, together with spices, glass, silver and paper. Yet the most valuable cargo was often invisible. Religions such as Buddhism and Islam, technologies like paper-making, musical instruments, and even fruits such as the peach travelled from one civilisation to another in merchants' caravans.

C. From the end of the fifteenth century, however, the caravans slowly vanished. European sailors had discovered sea routes to India and China, and moving goods by ship proved faster, cheaper and far safer than months of desert travel. The great trading cities of Central Asia gradually lost their wealth and importance.

D. In our century, the old idea has been reborn in a new form. Modern railways and motorways now follow the ancient directions, and freight trains regularly carry goods from China across Central Asia towards European markets. A new railway line through Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan is expected to shorten the journey even further.

E. The legend of the Silk Road now attracts a different kind of traveller. Tourists from all over the world come to walk through the restored squares of Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva, sleep in caravanserai-style hotels and photograph the same domes that traders saw five hundred years ago. Simpler visa rules have helped visitor numbers grow year after year.

F. This popularity, however, has a price. Millions of feet wear down ancient stairways, and unsuitable modern repairs can damage buildings that survived for centuries. Heritage experts argue that historic cities must find a careful balance between welcoming visitors and protecting the monuments those visitors come to see.

parts.passageText:
The Aral Sea: A Lesson for the World

In 1960 the Aral Sea was the fourth-largest lake on the planet, covering 68,000 square kilometres of territory between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. Around its shores stood busy fishing towns such as Moynaq, whose boats brought in tens of thousands of tonnes of fish every year and whose cannery supplied much of the Soviet Union.

The sea depended on two great rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya. In the 1960s, planners began redirecting their water into hundreds of canals to irrigate enormous new cotton fields. The results for agriculture were impressive; the results for the sea were catastrophic. Deprived of its rivers, the Aral began to retreat. By the 1990s it had split into separate parts, and by 2007 only about ten per cent of the original surface remained. Where fishing boats once sailed, camels now walk between rusting ships on dry sand.

The disappearance of the water destroyed far more than the fishing industry. Winds pick up salt and agricultural chemicals from the exposed seabed and carry them hundreds of kilometres, and doctors in the region report unusually high levels of breathing problems. The local climate has changed too: a large body of water softens temperatures, so without it summers have become hotter and winters colder.

Yet the story is not entirely hopeless. In 2005 Kazakhstan, supported by the World Bank, completed the Kokaral dam, which holds the Syr Darya's water in the northern part of the sea. Since then water levels there have risen by several metres, the water has become less salty, and fish — along with fishermen — have returned. The much larger southern section on the Uzbek side, however, is considered impossible to refill. Instead, Uzbekistan has chosen a different strategy: planting millions of hectares of drought-resistant saxaul trees on the dried seabed. Their roots hold the loose soil in place and reduce the dust storms at their source.

Scientists today describe the Aral Sea as one of the clearest warnings in environmental history: decisions taken without thinking about nature can undo, within a single human lifetime, what took thousands of years to create.

parts.passageText:
Tiny Forests, Big Hopes

On a grey corner of an industrial district in the Dutch city of Utrecht, something unusual is growing. Three years ago the site was a car park. (15) ______ Today the same plot holds more than forty species of trees and shrubs, and birdsong competes with the traffic noise.

This is a 'tiny forest' — a dense patch of native woodland no bigger than a tennis court. The method behind it was developed in the 1970s by the Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki. (16) ______ The result, supporters claim, is a wood that grows up to ten times faster than one planted in the traditional way.

The recipe sounds simple. First, the soil is dug deep and enriched with natural material. (17) ______ Because the young plants compete for light, they race upwards, forming a closed green roof within a few years.

The benefits go beyond beauty. (18) ______ In summer the shade makes the surrounding streets noticeably cooler, and in autumn the roots soak up rainwater that would otherwise flood the drains.

Scientists, however, warn against seeing tiny forests as a complete answer to climate change. (19) ______ A tennis-court-sized wood, they point out, stores in a decade roughly the carbon that a single passenger releases on one long-haul flight.

Even so, the movement keeps spreading, with thousands of plots now growing in the Netherlands, India, France and beyond. (20) ______ Schools in particular use them as open-air classrooms, where children measure insects and soil temperature instead of only reading about them.

Perhaps that is the real point. (21) ______ If a forest at the end of the street convinces a child that nature is worth protecting, it may achieve far more than its size suggests.

parts.passageText:
In Praise of Boredom

I recently watched a man wait four minutes for a bus. It was, apparently, an ordeal. In the first thirty seconds he checked his messages; in the next he refreshed a news feed that had not changed; by minute three he was watching a video of a stranger assembling furniture. At no point did he look up at the spring sky or simply stand and think. Waiting, once a natural part of every life, has become an emergency requiring immediate digital treatment.

We are the first generation in history that need never be bored, and we may come to regret it. Boredom is uncomfortable, which is precisely why it is useful. When the brain receives no entertainment, it entertains itself: it wanders, replays conversations, connects unrelated ideas, imagines futures. Psychologists call this the 'default mode', and it is where much of our most original thinking happens. Ask writers or scientists where their best ideas arrive, and the answers are suspiciously similar — in the shower, on a long walk, staring out of a train window. Rarely does anyone say 'while scrolling'.

The entertainment industry, of course, sees things differently. Every app on your phone is engineered by talented people whose salaries depend on you never experiencing an empty moment. They speak warmly of 'engagement', a word that sounds like commitment but means capture. I do not blame them — capturing attention is their job. I merely note that our attention is the prize in a contest we did not know we had entered, against opponents we cannot see, with rules written entirely by the other side.

Some argue that filling empty minutes with podcasts and articles is self-improvement, not distraction. There is something in this; a commute spent learning a language is hardly wasted. But improvement, too, can become a compulsion — the ambitious cousin of doom-scrolling. A mind that must always be fed is still a mind that cannot be left alone, whatever the quality of its diet.

I am not suggesting we abandon our phones and take up staring at walls professionally. Technology has returned to us hours that earlier generations lost to queues and paperwork, and only a hypocrite would type these words on a laptop and then demand you read them on paper. What I am suggesting is more modest: that we occasionally decline the rescue. Next time a bus is late, let it be late. Stand in the ordinary silence, be bored properly for five minutes, and see what your unsupervised mind drags home. It may be nothing. It may be the idea you have been too busy to have.

parts.passageText:
The Melting Water Towers of Central Asia

High above the farms and cities of Central Asia, the mountain ranges of the Tien Shan and the Pamir hold thousands of glaciers. Scientists often call these frozen reserves 'water towers', because they store winter snowfall as ice and release it gradually during hot, dry summers — precisely when the rivers below are needed most. The two great rivers of the region, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, both begin among these peaks, and tens of millions of people depend on their flow for drinking water, agriculture and electricity.

That dependable rhythm is now changing. By comparing modern satellite measurements with records kept by Soviet researchers since the mid-twentieth century, glaciologists have calculated that the Tien Shan has lost roughly a quarter of its ice mass since the 1960s. The rate of loss, moreover, appears to be accelerating: glaciers here are shrinking faster than the global average, partly because Central Asian summers have warmed sharply, and partly because dust and soot settle on the ice, darkening its surface so that it absorbs more sunlight instead of reflecting it.

Counter-intuitively, the first stage of glacier decline can look like abundance. As melting speeds up, rivers actually carry more water than before, encouraging farms and hydropower stations to expand. Hydrologists warn against reading this as good news. They describe a moment called 'peak water': the point at which a river's flow reaches its maximum and then begins a long, permanent decline as the ice reserve behind it runs out. Several major basins in the region are expected to pass this point around the middle of this century — within the lifetime of today's students.

What would that mean in practice? Agriculture consumes about ninety per cent of the region's water, much of it through open earth canals dug decades ago, from which a large share evaporates or leaks away before ever reaching a field. Even partial modernisation would soften the coming shortage considerably. Drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to a plant's roots through narrow pipes, can cut a farm's water use by up to half while actually raising yields, and Uzbekistan now subsidises farmers who install it. Meteorological stations are also being rebuilt in the high mountains, where data collection largely stopped after 1991, because forecasting future supply is impossible without knowing what is happening on the glaciers today.

The deeper challenge, researchers argue, is political rather than technical. Central Asia's rivers ignore national borders: water stored in the mountains of one state is consumed on the plains of another. Upstream countries prefer to release water in winter to generate electricity, while downstream countries need it in summer for their fields. Climate change raises the stakes of this old disagreement, but it may also supply the motivation to settle it. A river system approaching peak water, scientists observe, is an argument that nobody can afford to lose.

They protect the valleys from winter snowfall

answer.value: They store frozen water and release it during the dry season

answer.value: The extra water is a sign that the ice reserve is running out
